analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage to $5.50 an hour and ties future increases to the cost of living.
analysis.headline: The bill to raise the minimum wage to $5.50 an hour, with automatic cost-of-living increases, never left committee and never got a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would raise the federal minimum wage to $5.50 an hour starting in 1996 — up from the $4.25 in effect at the time — and then adjust it automatically each year for inflation, the same way Social Security benefits are adjusted. Today the minimum wage only rises when Congress passes a new law, which can take years, so its buying power erodes between increases. This bill would have ended that cycle. It was introduced on the first day of the new Congress by an independent Vermont lawmaker, referred to the House labor committee, sent to a subcommittee, and never heard from again.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers paid at or near the minimum wage — disproportionately women, teenagers, and adults in service and retail jobs — would see a direct raise, and the annual inflation adjustment would prevent the wage floor from losing value over time. Workers earning slightly above $5.50 would also tend to benefit as pay scales adjusted upward.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers paid at or near minimum wage

how_it_helps.text: Raises the federal minimum wage to $5.50 an hour after December 30, 1995.

Requires the wage to be adjusted each year, beginning in 1997, by the same cost-of-living formula used for Social Security benefits, so the minimum wage keeps pace with inflation without needing a new act of Congress.
The bill was introduced on the first day of the 104th Congress by Rep. Bernie Sanders and had 32 cosponsors, all House Democrats.

analysis.who_pays: Employers who pay minimum-wage wages — especially restaurants, retail stores, and other labor-intensive service businesses — would face higher payroll costs, and some of that cost would likely show up in prices. Small businesses operating on thin margins would bear the adjustment along with large chains.
analysis.who_pays_short: Restaurants, retail and other low-wage employers

drawbacks.text: The increase from $4.25 to $5.50 (about 29%) in a single step was larger than the eventual compromise Congress enacted in 1996 ($4.75, then $5.15), and opponents of minimum wage increases argue that a sharp jump raises costs for small businesses and can reduce hiring of entry-level workers.

Automatic inflation indexing is uncommon for the minimum wage; even supporters of higher minimums have at times preferred periodic legislative resets over a formula that operates with no congressional review.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For a full-time minimum-wage worker, the increase would have meant roughly $2,600 more per year before taxes, plus protection against erosion by inflation. The cost falls on employers of low-wage labor, partly passed to consumers. The main honest objection is the size and speed of the single-step increase; the inflation-indexing mechanism itself is a well-established approach (used for Social Security) that simply prevents the floor from shrinking between political fights. On balance, the direct gains to low-wage workers outweigh the diffuse costs spread across businesses and consumers.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House labor committee the day it was introduced, sent to a subcommittee three weeks later, and never advanced — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Bernie Sanders introduced the bill on January 4, 1995, the opening day of the 104th Congress.
The House referred it to the Committee on Economic and Educational Opportunities on the day of introduction.
On January 27, 1995, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections, where the action history ends.
No further action appears in the record through the end of the Congress on January 3, 1997 — the bill never received a committee vote or a floor vote.
Congress did eventually raise the minimum wage in 1996, but to a lower amount ($4.75 rising to $5.15) and without automatic inflation indexing.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Businesses that pay minimum-wage wages were better off because the bill died: no higher wage floor, and no automatic inflation increases that would have raised pay every year without a new vote. The eventual 1996 increase was smaller and lacked indexing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Low-wage employers; the bill never advanced

for.name: Rep. Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on the first day of the 104th Congress.

for.name: 32 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all 32 cosponsors were Democrats.

against.name: House Committee on Economic and Educational Opportunities
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day of introduction and never reported it out; no markup or hearing is recorded.

against.name: Rep. Bill Goodling
against.role: Chair, House Committee on Economic and Educational Opportunities
against.what_they_did: Led the committee to which the bill was referred during the 104th Congress; the bill never advanced past a subcommittee referral under his chairmanship.

against.name: Subcommittee on Workforce Protections
against.what_they_did: Held the bill from January 27, 1995 onward with no recorded action.

sides.party_line_note: All 32 cosponsors were House Democrats and the sponsor was an Independent; no Republican support is recorded, and the Republican-majority committee of referral took no action.

industries.note: Among the largest employers of minimum-wage workers; a $5.50 floor plus automatic annual increases would have raised their payroll costs indefinitely. Their interest in defeating the bill ran directly against the wage gains workers would have received.

industries.industry: Retail and other low-wage service employers
industries.note: Would have borne the same higher wage floor and the inflation indexing that removes future bargaining over the minimum. The benefit to their lowest-paid workers was the cost these employers avoided when the bill died.
